claims.claim: A near-universal one-child limit was imposed in China in 1980 and written into the constitution in 1982.
claims.episode_span: The policy was formally announced in 1980 and written into the constitution in 1982.
claims.supporting_quote: A near-universal one-child limit was imposed in 1980 and written into the country's constitution in 1982.

claims.claim: On 1 January 2016 the one-child policy was replaced by a universal two-child policy.
claims.episode_span: the central government ended the one-child limit and introduced a universal two-child policy effective 1 January 2016
claims.supporting_quote: On 1 January 2016, the one-child policy was replaced by the two-child policy .

claims.claim: Song Jian, the leading advocate of the one-child modeling, was a control theorist at the Ministry of Aerospace Industry known for his career in missile science, working with engineers trained in cybernetics.
claims.episode_span: most prominently missile scientist Song Jian, applied cybernetic models borrowed from military planning
claims.supporting_quote: The leader of the group, Song Jian , was a control theorist at the Ministry of Aerospace Industry. He was known for his career in missile science.

claims.claim: Song Jian's group calculated an ideal population for China of 700 million and argued a universal one-child policy was required to reach it.
claims.episode_span: would bring the total population down to an “optimal” 700 million by the middle of the twenty-first century
claims.supporting_quote: Song determined that the ideal population of China was 700 million, and that a universal one-child policy for all would be required to meet that goal.

claims.claim: China's sex ratio at birth reached 117 males per 100 females and stabilized at that level between 2000 and 2013, about 10% above the natural baseline.
claims.episode_span: By the 2000 census the national ratio had reached 117 boys for every 100 girls
claims.supporting_quote: The sex ratio of a newborn infant (between male and female births) in mainland China reached 117:100, and stabilized between 2000 and 2013

claims.claim: China's fertility restrictions produced a deficit of roughly 40 million female babies, mostly through sex-selective abortion.
claims.episode_span: large enough to remove an estimated 30 to 40 million females from the population over three decades
claims.supporting_quote: Fertility restrictions also had unintended consequences such as a deficit of 40 million female babies, most of which was due to sex-selective abortion

claims.claim: From the mid-1980s rural parents were allowed a second child if the first was a daughter, and ethnic minorities under 10 million people were granted exceptions.
claims.episode_span: rural families whose first child was a girl were often permitted a second birth after a waiting period, while ethnic minorities and some frontier regions were largely exempt
claims.supporting_quote: In the mid-1980s, rural parents were allowed to have a second child if the first was a daughter. It also allowed exceptions for some other groups, including ethnic minorities under 10 million people.

claims.claim: The Chinese government credits the policy with preventing 400 million births, an estimate some scholars dispute.
claims.episode_span: official reports credited the policy with preventing several hundred million births
claims.supporting_quote: says that it prevented 400 million births, although some scholars dispute that estimate
